title: Causal LM Pretraining
summary: Train a transformer to predict the next token on raw text — the foundation step behind every base LLM.
details: Causal language modeling trains a decoder-only transformer on raw text with a simple objective: given all previous tokens, predict the next one, minimizing cross-entropy loss. No labels are needed, so training scales to trillions of tokens. Architecture, data mixture, and the 6*N*D FLOPs scaling relationship (Kaplan/Chinchilla) determine the outcome. The result is a base model with broad knowledge but no instruction-following behavior — that comes later with fine-tuning.
data_needs: Trillions of tokens of raw text

demo.title: Next-token loss on toy logits
demo.program:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)
logits = torch.randn(2, 6, 1000)   # batch, seq, vocab
targets = torch.randint(0, 1000, (2, 6))
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, 1000), targets.reshape(-1))
print("causal LM loss:", round(float(loss), 3))

title: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
summary: Fine-tune a base model on instruction-response pairs so it follows instructions.
details: SFT takes a pretrained base model and continues training on curated (instruction, response) pairs, computing loss only on the response tokens (prompt tokens are masked with -100). Typical setups use a small learning rate (1e-5 to 2e-5), a few epochs, and packing of short examples. SFT converts a base model into an assistant that follows instructions, but it only imitates the demonstration distribution — it does not learn preferences beyond the demos, which is why RLHF/DPO usually follow.

demo.title: Masked SFT loss (prompt masked)
demo.program:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
logits = torch.randn(2, 8, 32000)
labels = torch.randint(0, 32000, (2, 8))
labels[:, :4] = -100  # mask the prompt tokens
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, 32000), labels.reshape(-1),
                       ignore_index=-100)
print("SFT loss:", round(float(loss), 3))

title: RLHF with PPO
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model, then optimize the policy with PPO under a KL penalty.
details: RLHF has three stages: (1) SFT on demonstrations, (2) train a reward model on human preference pairs (chosen vs rejected), (3) optimize the policy with PPO against the reward model, penalizing KL divergence from the SFT model to prevent reward hacking. PPO's clipped surrogate objective keeps updates stable. RLHF produced ChatGPT's helpful tone, but it is finicky — reward over-optimization and training instability are the classic failure modes.

demo.title: PPO clipped objective sketch
demo.program:
import torch
ratio = torch.tensor([1.1, 0.9, 1.3])      # pi_new/pi_old
adv = torch.tensor([0.5, -0.2, 0.8])       # advantages
eps = 0.2
clipped = torch.clamp(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps)
loss = -torch.min(ratio * adv, clipped * adv).mean()
print("PPO loss:", round(float(loss), 4))

title: DPO
summary: Direct Preference Optimization: align on preference pairs with a simple classification loss — no reward model, no PPO.
details: DPO reframes RLHF as supervised learning: given a (prompt, chosen, rejected) triple, it directly increases the log-probability margin of the chosen response over the rejected one, relative to a frozen reference model. The loss is -log sigmoid(beta * margin). DPO is dramatically simpler and more stable than PPO-based RLHF and matches it on many benchmarks, though very large-scale runs sometimes still prefer online RL. Variants (IPO, KTO, ORPO) tweak the objective.

demo.title: DPO loss on toy log-probs
demo.program:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
def dpo_loss(pi_c, pi_r, ref_c, ref_r, beta=0.1):
    margin = (pi_c - ref_c) - (pi_r - ref_r)
    return -F.logsigmoid(beta * margin).mean()
l = dpo_loss(torch.tensor([-0.5]), torch.tensor([-1.2]),
             torch.tensor([-0.6]), torch.tensor([-1.0]))
print("DPO loss:", round(float(l), 4))

title: ORPO
summary: Odds-Ratio Preference Optimization: SFT and preference alignment in a single stage, no reference model.
details: ORPO folds preference alignment into the SFT stage itself: the loss combines standard next-token loss on the chosen response with an odds-ratio penalty that pushes down the rejected response — all without a separate reference model. It is a one-stage, reference-free alternative to the SFT-then-DPO pipeline, attractive when you want alignment in a single training run. Trade-off: it couples imitation and preference learning, which can complicate debugging.

demo.title: ORPO odds-ratio term sketch
demo.program:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
logp_chosen, logp_rejected = torch.tensor([-0.4]), torch.tensor([-1.5])
odds_c = torch.exp(logp_chosen) / (1 - torch.exp(logp_chosen) + 1e-9)
odds_r = torch.exp(logp_rejected) / (1 - torch.exp(logp_rejected) + 1e-9)
or_loss = -torch.log(torch.sigmoid(torch.log(odds_c / odds_r)))
print("odds-ratio loss:", round(float(or_loss), 4))

title: KTO
summary: Kahneman-Tversky Optimization: learn from unpaired good/bad examples using prospect-theory-style loss.
details: KTO drops the requirement for paired preferences: it learns from binary feedback (this response was good / bad) using a loss inspired by prospect theory — humans weigh losses more than gains, so the loss is asymmetric around a reference point. This matches real product data (thumbs up/down) far better than paired triples. KTO often matches DPO with cheaper, more abundant data.

demo.title: KTO-style asymmetric weighting
demo.program:
good = [0.8, 0.9, 0.7]   # rewards for liked responses
bad = [0.2, 0.3]             # rewards for disliked responses
lam_good, lam_bad = 1.0, 1.5  # losses weigh more (prospect theory)
score = lam_good*sum(good)/len(good) - lam_bad*(1-sum(bad)/len(bad))
print("KTO-style score:", round(score, 3))

title: Knowledge Distillation
summary: Train a small student model to mimic a large teacher's outputs or logits.
details: In distillation, a large teacher model generates soft targets (logit distributions) or outputs for training inputs, and a smaller student trains to match them — often with a temperature-scaled KL divergence loss mixed with hard-label loss. The student can reach near-teacher quality at a fraction of the size (the recipe behind DistilBERT, TinyLlama-style models, and DeepSeek-R1 distills). Data can be teacher-generated, so the method also distills reasoning traces, not just labels.
data_needs: Inputs for the teacher to label (or teacher-generated)

demo.title: Temperature-scaled distillation loss
demo.program:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
T = 2.0
teacher_logits = torch.randn(4, 100)
student_logits = torch.randn(4, 100)
p = F.softmax(teacher_logits / T, dim=-1)
q = F.log_softmax(student_logits / T, dim=-1)
loss = F.kl_div(q, p, reduction="batchmean") * T * T
print("distill loss:", round(float(loss), 3))

provenance: Hinton et al. (2015); modern LLM distills

title: Curriculum Learning
summary: Order training examples from easy to hard so the model builds on mastered skills.
details: Curriculum learning presents examples in order of increasing difficulty — short sentences before long documents, arithmetic before algebra. The classic implementation scores example difficulty (length, rarity, model loss) and schedules sampling probability over training. It can speed convergence and improve final quality, though modern LLM pretraining often uses implicit curricula (data mixture schedules) rather than explicit per-example ordering.
data_needs: Difficulty scores or labels per example

demo.title: Difficulty-based sampler
demo.program:
import random
random.seed(0)
examples = [(f"ex{i}", d) for i, d in enumerate([1, 5, 2, 9, 3, 8])]
examples.sort(key=lambda e: e[1])          # easy first
schedule = examples[:3] + examples          # warm up on easy, then all
print("first 5 in schedule:", [e[0] for e in schedule[:5]])

title: Instruction Tuning
summary: Fine-tune on a broad mixture of tasks phrased as instructions to get zero-shot generalization.
details: Instruction tuning (FLAN, T0) fine-tunes a model on hundreds of NLP tasks, each phrased as a natural-language instruction with input and target. The key finding: training on many tasks improves zero-shot performance on held-out tasks — the model learns to follow instructions generally, not just memorize tasks. It is the bridge between base pretraining and assistant behavior, usually preceding RLHF.

demo.title: Task-mixture batch builder
demo.program:
import random
random.seed(1)
tasks = {"qa": 1000, "summarize": 800, "translate": 600, "classify": 900}
total = sum(tasks.values())
batch = random.choices(list(tasks), weights=tasks.values(), k=8)
print("mixed batch:", batch)

title: Continued Pretraining
summary: Keep pretraining a base model on domain text (code, medicine, law) to inject expertise.
details: Continued (domain-adaptive) pretraining resumes the causal-LM objective on domain corpora — e.g., PubMed for medicine, legal opinions for law — before any instruction tuning. It reliably boosts domain benchmarks but risks catastrophic forgetting of general ability; practitioners mix in 10-30% general data ('replay') and use lower learning rates. It is how specialized models (BioMedLM, SaulLM) are born.
data_needs: Billions of domain tokens + replay mix

demo.title: Domain/general replay mixture
demo.program:
domain, general = 0.8, 0.2
steps = 10000
print(f"domain steps: {int(steps*domain)}, replay steps: {int(steps*general)}")

title: Model Merging
summary: Combine fine-tuned models by averaging weights (SLERP, TIES) — no extra training.
details: Model merging fuses two or more fine-tunes of the same base by combining weights: simple averaging, spherical interpolation (SLERP), or TIES (which resolves sign conflicts and prunes small deltas). Merged models often inherit capabilities from both parents — e.g., a chat model merged with a code model. It costs nothing but inference-time arithmetic, making it the cheapest 'training' method in the book.

demo.title: SLERP merge of two toy weight vectors
demo.program:
import torch, math
a = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0]); b = torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0])
t = 0.5
omega = math.acos(float(a @ b) / (a.norm() * b.norm()))
merged = (math.sin((1-t)*omega)*a + math.sin(t*omega)*b) / math.sin(omega)
print("merged:", [round(float(x), 3) for x in merged])

title: Mixed Precision Training
summary: Train in FP16/BF16 with FP32 master weights — ~2x faster, half the memory.
details: Mixed precision keeps a master copy of weights in FP32 but computes forward/backward passes in FP16 or BF16, scaling the loss to avoid underflow (FP16) or relying on BF16's wider range. With torch.amp it is nearly free: autocast regions plus a gradient scaler. BF16 is now preferred for LLMs (no loss scaling needed). Combined with activation checkpointing and sharding, it is what makes large-model training fit in memory.

demo.title: Memory math: BF16 vs FP32
demo.program:
params = 7e9
for dtype, b in [("fp32", 4), ("bf16", 2)]:
    gb = params * b / 1e9
    print(f"{dtype}: weights {gb:.0f} GB | +optimizer states ~{gb*2:.0f} GB (Adam fp32)")

title: Gradient Accumulation
summary: Simulate large batch sizes by accumulating gradients over micro-batches.
details: When GPU memory cannot hold the target batch, gradient accumulation runs several smaller micro-batches, sums their gradients, and steps the optimizer once — mathematically equivalent to one large batch (for most optimizers). It trades wall-clock time for memory and is universal in LLM training configs. Caveat: batch-norm-style layers and some schedulers need care, but transformers are accumulation-friendly.

demo.title: Accumulate grads over micro-batches
demo.program:
import torch
model = torch.nn.Linear(10, 1)
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
opt.zero_grad()
for _ in range(4):  # 4 micro-batches = 4x effective batch
    loss = model(torch.randn(8, 10)).pow(2).mean() / 4
    loss.backward()
opt.step()
print("stepped once over 4 micro-batches")

title: ZeRO / FSDP Sharding
summary: Shard optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across GPUs to train models bigger than one card.
details: ZeRO (DeepSpeed) and FSDP (PyTorch) shard training state across data-parallel workers: stage 1 shards optimizer states, stage 2 adds gradients, stage 3 shards parameters themselves, gathering them just-in-time via all-gather. A 7B model needing ~100+ GB with Adam fits across 8x40GB cards with ZeRO-3. It is the default for multi-GPU LLM training, usually combined with mixed precision and activation checkpointing.

demo.title: ZeRO-3 memory estimate

title: Activation Checkpointing
summary: Trade recomputation for memory: drop activations, recompute them on the backward pass.
details: Activation (gradient) checkpointing saves only a subset of layer activations during the forward pass and recomputes the rest during backprop — cutting activation memory by 5-10x at ~30% extra compute. It is what lets long-context and large-model training fit at all. Selective checkpointing (every Nth layer) tunes the trade-off; combined with FlashAttention's IO-awareness, memory stops being the binding constraint.

demo.title: Checkpointing trade-off math
demo.program:
layers, act_per_layer_gb = 32, 1.5
full = layers * act_per_layer_gb
ckpt_every = 4
saved = (layers // ckpt_every) * act_per_layer_gb
print(f"full: {full} GB -> checkpointed: {saved} GB "
      f"({full/saved:.1f}x less, ~30% more compute)")

title: Cosine LR Scheduling
summary: Warm up the learning rate, decay it with a cosine curve — the standard LLM schedule.
details: The canonical LLM schedule: linear warmup (e.g., 1-3% of steps) from 0 to peak LR, then cosine decay to ~10% of peak over the remaining steps. Warmup avoids early instability; cosine decay gives a smooth landing that improves final loss versus step decay. Variants (warmup-stable-decay, cosine with restarts) tune the tail, but plain warmup+cosine remains the default in nearly every open training recipe.

demo.title: Cosine schedule values

title: Data Packing
summary: Pack multiple short documents into each training sequence to stop wasting padding.
details: Naive batching pads every sequence to the max length, wasting compute on pad tokens. Packing concatenates short documents (with attention masks or document separators) to fill each 2048/4096-token slot nearly full. It typically recovers 10-30% of training throughput on short-document mixes like instruction data. Implementation detail: use block-diagonal attention or reset position IDs per document to avoid cross-document leakage.

demo.title: Packing efficiency gain
demo.program:
import random
random.seed(0)
seq_len = 2048
docs = [random.randint(50, 600) for _ in range(200)]
padded = len(docs) * seq_len
packed, cur = 0, 0
for d in docs:
    if cur + d > seq_len: packed += 1; cur = 0
    cur += d
packed += 1
print(f"padded seqs worth: {padded/seq_len:.0f} -> packed: {packed} "
      f"({padded/seq_len/packed:.1f}x less waste)")

title: Constitutional AI
summary: Self-critique against a written constitution: the model revises its own outputs, then trains on the revisions.
details: Constitutional AI (Anthropic) replaces some human labeling with AI feedback: the model generates a response, critiques it against a written list of principles (the 'constitution'), revises it, and the (original, revised) pairs become preference data for RL. It scales alignment without proportional human labeling and bakes principles explicitly into training. The constitution itself becomes an auditable artifact of the model's values.

demo.title: Self-critique loop sketch
demo.program:
constitution = ["be honest", "do not stereotype", "explain reasoning"]
draft = "All X are Y, obviously."
critique = [p for p in constitution]  # model checks draft vs each principle
revised = "Some X tend to be Y, though it varies; here is why..."
print("principles checked:", len(critique))
print("revised:", revised[:40], "...")

title: Reward Modeling
summary: Train a model to score responses so RL can optimize against it.
details: A reward model is typically a pretrained LLM with a scalar head, trained on human preference pairs with a Bradley-Terry loss: it learns to assign higher scores to chosen responses. The RM is the steering wheel of RLHF — its quality caps the whole pipeline. Practitioners track RM accuracy on held-out pairs, calibrate for length bias (RMs love verbosity), and ensemble multiple RMs to resist hacking.

demo.title: Bradley-Terry preference loss
demo.program:
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
r_chosen = torch.tensor([1.2, 0.8]); r_rejected = torch.tensor([0.4, 0.9])
loss = -F.logsigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected).mean()
acc = (r_chosen > r_rejected).float().mean()
print(f"loss={float(loss):.3f} acc={float(acc):.0%}")

title: RLVR
summary: RL with verifiable rewards: reinforce only on answers checkable by code or math.
details: RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) applies RL only where correctness is mechanically checkable — math answers, unit tests, formal proofs. The reward is 1 if the verifier accepts, 0 otherwise: no learned reward model, no hacking surface. DeepSeek-R1 showed RVR-style RL can elicit long chain-of-thought reasoning emergently. Limitation: it only works in verifiable domains, so open-ended quality still needs human-preference methods.

demo.title: Verifiable reward

title: MoE Load-Balancing Loss
summary: The auxiliary loss that keeps mixture-of-experts routers from collapsing onto a few experts.
details: In MoE training, a router assigns each token to top-k experts; without intervention it collapses, sending everything to 2-3 experts. The load-balancing auxiliary loss penalizes uneven expert utilization (e.g., Switch Transformer loss or expert-choice routing), keeping all experts trained. Coefficient tuning matters: too strong hurts quality, too weak wastes experts. It is the small loss term that makes trillion-parameter MoEs trainable.

demo.title: Load-balance loss sketch
demo.program:
import torch
tokens_per_expert = torch.tensor([90., 5., 3., 2.])   # collapsed!
frac = tokens_per_expert / tokens_per_expert.sum()
aux = (frac * torch.tensor([0.25]*4)).sum() * 4       # want uniform
print("aux loss (collapsed):", round(float(aux), 3))

title: Sparse / Pruning-Aware Training
summary: Train with sparsity in mind so the model prunes cleanly afterward.
details: Instead of training dense then pruning (which shocks the model), sparsity-aware training keeps weights sparse throughout — via gradual magnitude pruning schedules, sparse momentum, or 2:4 structured sparsity that NVIDIA hardware accelerates. The model learns representations robust to pruning, so the final sparse model keeps most of its accuracy. It is how production models hit latency budgets without full retraining.

demo.title: Magnitude pruning sketch
demo.program:
import torch
w = torch.randn(1000)
keep = int(0.5 * w.numel())
thresh = torch.topk(w.abs(), keep).values.min()
sparse = torch.where(w.abs() >= thresh, w, torch.zeros_like(w))
print(f"sparsity: {(sparse == 0).float().mean():.0%}")

title: Synthetic Data Training
summary: Generate training data with a stronger model, then train on it — the self-improvement loop.
details: When human data runs out, strong models generate synthetic data: solutions, instructions, dialogues, or tool-use traces, filtered by verifiers or model judges. Phi, WizardLM, and the OpenHermes lineage are synthetic-data success stories. The risks are well documented: model collapse (training on your own outputs narrows diversity), inherited biases, and benchmark contamination — so pipelines dedup, filter, and mix synthetic with real data.
data_needs: Seed prompts + a strong generator model

demo.title: Synthetic data quality gate
demo.program:
import random
random.seed(2)
gen = [{"q": f"q{i}", "a": f"a{i}", "judge": random.random()} for i in range(10)]
kept = [g for g in gen if g["judge"] > 0.7]
print(f"kept {len(kept)}/{len(gen)} after judge filter")

title: Weight Decay
summary: Penalize large weights during optimization — the quiet regularizer in every LLM recipe.
details: Weight decay (typically AdamW with 0.01-0.1) adds an L2 penalty pulling weights toward zero, curbing overfitting and stabilizing long runs. AdamW's decoupled formulation applies decay outside the adaptive update, which is why it replaced L2-in-Adam. It interacts with the learning rate schedule — decay too hard and the model underfits; too soft and late-training loss plateaus higher. Small knob, big cumulative effect over trillions of tokens.

demo.title: AdamW decoupled decay step
demo.program:
import torch
w = torch.tensor([1.0, -2.0]); lr, wd = 0.01, 0.1
grad = torch.tensor([0.1, 0.1])
w = w - lr * (grad + wd * w)   # decay decoupled from adaptive term
print("updated:", [round(float(x), 4) for x in w])

title: Checkpoint Averaging (EMA/SWA)
summary: Average recent checkpoints for a free robustness and quality boost.
details: Averaging the last N checkpoints (or an exponential moving average of weights) smooths out late-training noise and often improves eval scores by a point or two — for free. SWA (stochastic weight averaging) extends the idea across the LR schedule's tail. Nearly every serious release averages: it is the cheapest quality gain in training, and the averaged weights also serve as a more stable base for fine-tuning.

demo.title: Average three checkpoints
demo.program:
import torch
ckpts = [torch.randn(5) for _ in range(3)]
avg = sum(ckpts) / len(ckpts)
print("averaged:", [round(float(x), 3) for x in avg])
